prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "INTEL CORP" (ticker INTC), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "INTC", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Intel Corporation
result.industry: Semiconductors (CPUs, AI chips and contract chip manufacturing)
markets: Data center CPUs and AI systems (Xeon 6/6+, Gaudi, Crescent Island)
Contract chip manufacturing and advanced packaging (Intel Foundry: 18A, 14A, Foveros/EMIB)
Driver-assistance and self-driving chips (Mobileye, majority owned)

mission.statement: We create world-changing technology that improves the life of every person on the planet.
mission.plain: Intel wants to invent and build chips that make life better for everyone in the world.

about.plain: Intel designs the main brain chips (processors) inside most of the world's laptops, desktops and internet servers. Unlike most chip companies, it also owns giant factories in the US, Ireland and Israel where it builds those chips itself. It is now trying to build chips for other companies too, the way TSMC does. It also owns most of Mobileye, which makes chips that help cars see the road.
about.customers: PC makers like Dell, HP and Lenovo, cloud and enterprise server buyers, carmakers, and a small but growing set of outside companies that pay Intel to manufacture their chips.
about.everyday: The 'Intel Inside' sticker on millions of laptops means the main processor was made by Intel.

money.plain: Core Ultra processors for laptops and desktops (Client Computing Group, $32.2B in 2025)
Xeon server processors and AI accelerators ($16.9B in 2025; up 59% year on year in Q2 2026)
Driver-assistance chips for cars (Mobileye) plus other small businesses; Altera was sold down to 49% in Sept 2025
Intel Foundry building chips on 18A/14A and packaging them for outside customers ($293M outside revenue in Q2 2026)
Chips and OpenVINO software for robots, factories and smart devices, part of the renamed Client Computing and Physical AI Group

result.summary: Intel still has real advantages: the x86 duopoly with AMD, deep relationships with every PC and server maker, and the only leading-edge chip factories run by a US company, now backed by the US government (about a 10% stake), NVIDIA ($5B) and SoftBank. But it has lost manufacturing leadership to TSMC and a third of the server market to AMD, revenue fell from $79.0B in 2021 to $52.9B in 2025, and its foundry has yet to win a large outside customer, so its moat is narrower and less certain than a decade ago. A 2026 AI-driven CPU shortage has restored growth (Q2 2026 revenue +25%) and pricing.

pricingPower.evidence: With server CPUs in short supply from agentic-AI demand in 2026, Intel raised prices: reported Q2 2026 client average selling prices rose about 27% and server prices about 48% year on year while revenue grew 25% to $16.1B and GAAP gross margin recovered to 40.4%; but in 2022-2024 it had to discount heavily against AMD and gross margin fell from 56.0% (2020) to 32.7% (2024).

moats.evidence: 'Intel Inside' remains one of the best-known technology brands and Intel holds one of only two x86 licences plus a huge patent portfolio, though the brand's reputation for leadership was damaged by years of process delays.

Decades of software and enterprise validation are tuned for Intel x86 and its vPro management tools, but software runs unchanged on AMD x86, so switching to AMD is easy, and Arm chips are increasingly viable.
The x86 software ecosystem benefits Intel, but it is shared with AMD, and Intel's AI software (oneAPI, OpenVINO) has nothing like NVIDIA's CUDA community.
Intel ships hundreds of millions of CPUs a year and owns its fabs, but its manufacturing cost has been above TSMC's and Intel Foundry lost about $2.1B in Q2 2026 alone.

Leading-edge logic manufacturing is down to three players (TSMC, Samsung, Intel), and Intel is the only US-headquartered one, which gives it a protected role in US government Secure Enclave and CHIPS Act programs.
Offering a non-Taiwan, US-based leading-edge foundry is a differentiated pitch, but it has so far drawn little outside revenue (about $112M excluding Altera in Q2 2026).

Intel is one of very few companies able to develop leading-edge processes (18A with RibbonFET and PowerVia backside power, the first High-NA EUV production with ASML) and advanced packaging (Foveros, EMIB), though it fell years behind TSMC between 2016 and 2023.
Its US fabs in Arizona, Oregon, New Mexico and Ohio are strategic national assets, reflected in the US government's roughly 10% equity stake taken in August 2025.

customers.evidence: PC makers keep Intel as their main CPU supplier (about 71% of x86 notebooks in Q2 2026 per Mercury Research) and Panther Lake reviews were good, but customers defected steadily to AMD in servers (Intel's x86 unit share fell from about 94% in 2020 to about 66%), and Raptor Lake instability problems in 2024 hurt trust.

talent.evidence: Intel has a deep engineering bench and Lip-Bu Tan has recruited senior leaders (e.g. new CTO and CCPG head in 2026), but it cut roughly a fifth of its workforce in 2024-2025, ended some perks, and lost engineers to NVIDIA, AMD and Apple, which pay more in stock.

product.evidence: Core Ultra Series 3 (Panther Lake, Intel 18A) and Xeon 6/6+ are competitive and in short supply in 2026, but AMD's EPYC and Ryzen X3D still win many performance benchmarks, Apple's M-series leads laptop efficiency, and Intel's Gaudi AI chips failed to gain traction against NVIDIA.

competitors.name: Advanced Micro Devices
competitors.note: x86 server (EPYC vs Xeon) and PC processors (Ryzen vs Core), GPUs and FPGAs

competitors.name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing
competitors.note: Leading-edge contract manufacturing and advanced packaging (N2/A16 vs 18A/14A); also makes Intel's own outsourced chips

competitors.name: NVIDIA
competitors.note: AI data center accelerators, Grace Arm CPUs, and Arm PC chips with MediaTek; also an Intel investor and partner on custom x86 CPUs

competitors.name: Qualcomm
competitors.note: Snapdragon X Arm laptop processors and planned data center chips

competitors.name: Apple
competitors.note: Replaced Intel with its own M-series chips in Macs in 2020-2023 (reported in 2026 as a possible Intel foundry customer)

competitors.name: Samsung Electronics
competitors.note: Leading-edge foundry (2nm) competing for the same outside customers

competitors.name: Arm Holdings
competitors.note: Arm architecture licensed to rivals erodes x86 in PCs and servers

competitors.name: Amazon (AWS Graviton)
competitors.note: In-house Arm Graviton server CPUs and Trainium AI chips displace Xeon in AWS

competitors.name: Alphabet (Google Axion, TPU)
competitors.note: In-house Axion Arm CPUs and TPUs reduce Google Cloud's need for Xeon and Gaudi

competitors.name: Microsoft (Cobalt, Maia)
competitors.note: In-house Cobalt Arm CPUs for Azure, though also a planned Intel 18A foundry customer

competitors.name: Broadcom
competitors.note: Custom AI ASICs and data center networking/Ethernet

competitors.name: MediaTek
competitors.note: Arm PC chips (with NVIDIA) and Chromebook processors

competitors.name: GlobalFoundries
competitors.note: US-based contract manufacturing on mature nodes

competitors.name: Chinese CPU and AI chip makers (Huawei HiSilicon, Hygon, Loongson)
competitors.note: Domestic Chinese CPUs and AI chips replace Intel in China, one of Intel's largest markets by billing

competitors.name: NXP Semiconductors
competitors.note: Driver-assistance and automotive chips competing with Mobileye

threats: Intel Foundry may fail to sign large outside 14A customers (Lip-Bu Tan has said 14A could be dropped without one), leaving huge fixed costs; foundry lost about $2.1B in Q2 2026
AMD keeps taking server and PC share (Intel x86 server unit share fell from ~94% in 2020 to ~66% in Q2 2026)
Arm-based chips from Apple, Qualcomm, NVIDIA/MediaTek, AWS Graviton, Google Axion and Microsoft Cobalt shrink the x86 market
AI spending flows mostly to NVIDIA GPUs and custom ASICs, where Intel has little share after Gaudi underperformed
Heavy capex (2026 guided above $20B, 2027 'significantly above') with total debt of about $50.5B; management says it may need to tap capital markets
Elon Musk's Terafab, Intel's highest-profile 14A prospect, is also negotiating with TSMC
US government (about 10% holder) and political involvement, plus China exposure and export controls
The 2026 CPU shortage and price rises may reverse when supply catches up

ceo.name: Lip-Bu Tan
ceo.background: Physics BS (Nanyang University), MS nuclear engineering (MIT), MBA (University of San Francisco); founded Walden International VC; CEO of Cadence Design Systems 2009-2021

c1.evidence: Intel leads the mature x86 CPU market by units, but it is not the leader in the fast-growing AI accelerator or leading-edge foundry markets, which NVIDIA and TSMC dominate.

c2.evidence: Customers pick Intel for supply availability, broad PC-maker partnerships, x86 compatibility and now a US-based supply chain, but AMD offers the same x86 compatibility and often better performance, so the advantage is copyable.

c3.evidence: Nearly everyone recognises 'Intel Inside' and it remains the volume leader in PC chips, but it is no longer seen as the default best choice by enthusiasts, many of whom recommend AMD or Apple silicon.

c4.evidence: Intel's purpose is 'We create world-changing technology that improves the life of every person on the planet', and rebuilding US leading-edge chipmaking would matter strategically, but recent management focus has been survival, cost cuts and capital raising.

c6.evidence: “legacy, struggling, comeback, American chipmaker” — the impression has been mostly negative since 2020 because of delays and losses, but turned more hopeful in 2026 as the stock roughly tripled on AI CPU demand and foundry deal hopes.

c7.evidence: AI agents running on CPUs, AI PCs and the global foundry market (TSMC alone sells well over $100B a year) are large, growing markets, and analysts expect Intel revenue to rise about 19% in 2026 to $63.1B.

c8.evidence: Foundry services for outside chip designers (Terafab, Microsoft, US Defense Secure Enclave), advanced packaging, physical AI/robotics and inference GPUs (Crescent Island) are big new markets for Intel's technology.

m1.evidence: Lip-Bu Tan has a clear plan (engineering-first culture, customer-driven foundry, AI systems with partners like NVIDIA and SambaNova), but it is a turnaround plan more than a new vision of the future.

m2.evidence: Not Intel's founder (he founded Walden International), but he invested about $25M of his own money in Intel stock after joining and is known for a relentless work schedule.

m4.evidence: He talks constantly about listening to customers and cut management layers, but he also oversaw deep layoffs and stricter office and perk policies.

m5.evidence: He is trying to rebuild an engineering-first culture, flattening the organisation and bringing in new technical leaders, but it is too early to see a stream of new inventions.

m6.evidence: With degrees in physics and nuclear engineering and 12 years running chip-design software maker Cadence, he personally reviews chip designs and customer engagements.

m7.evidence: He is a long-time church elder and philanthropist (CMU professorships, S$3M to NTU for AI), though his past China investments drew political criticism in 2025.

m7b.evidence: No top-university commencement address found; he received honorary doctorates from the University of San Francisco (2022) and Carnegie Mellon (2025), where Sal Khan gave the address.

m8b.evidence: He is a low-key, soft-spoken operator and investor rather than a flamboyant public personality.

m9.evidence: At Cadence he more than doubled revenue and the stock multiplied many times over; at Intel, revenue grew 25% in Q2 2026 and the company beat guidance repeatedly, but foundry still loses billions.

m10.evidence: Tan cut operating expenses sharply in 2025, removed management layers, cancelled fab projects in Germany and Poland and slowed Ohio to conserve cash.

c10.evidence: Intel processors run a large share of the world's PCs and servers, powering work, school, banking and the internet for billions of people.

p2.evidence: Developing and manufacturing 2nm-class chips (18A, 14A with High-NA EUV) is one of the hardest industrial tasks in the world, and Intel is the only US company doing it.

f2.evidence: Gross margin fell from 56.0% in 2020 to 34.8% in 2025 and operating margin from 30.4% to -4.2%.

f3.evidence: At June 27, 2026 Intel had $29.7B of cash and short-term investments against $50.5B of debt, with positive equity of $103.1B but 2025 operating cash flow of only $9.7B against heavy capex.

f4.evidence: Operating income fell from $23.7B (2020) to a $2.2B loss (2025) and operating cash flow from $35.4B to $9.7B.

v1.evidence: Intel chips are good and widely available, but there is no simple reason to pick them over AMD's Ryzen/EPYC or Apple's M-series in most uses.

v2.evidence: Intel was long a respected employer, but repeated layoffs since 2024 have hurt morale and it no longer appears near the top of rankings such as Glassdoor's Best Places to Work.

c5.evidence: If Intel vanished, PC makers, the US government and every company that needs non-Asian leading-edge manufacturing would lose a key supplier, causing chip shortages, though AMD and TSMC could fill most demand over time.
